children: By Nat Ives, WSJ Leadership Institute
Good morning. I promise it wasn't a setup.

Almost as soon as this newsletter yesterday name-dropped Dyson's Airwrap as a successful brand extension, the company rolled out another highly engineered device in yet another new category: an AI-powered toothbrush that promises to floss your teeth while you brush.

The company's CameraJet is the first foray into oral care for Dyson, best known for its "no loss of suction" vacuum cleaners, the WSJ Leadership Institute's Katie Deighton writes. Inventor and company owner James Dyson hadn't worked with water since he codesigned the Rotork Sea Truck as a student at London's Royal College of Art.
"This is something completely new. But why not?" he said to Katie in a video call from his superyacht, Nahlin, after spending six years on the creation.
The CameraJet is also a $499 entry-not counting the cost of the necessary Dyson toothpaste-to a large, saturated and not-especially-fast-growing category.
I had a couple of questions for Katie.

Dyson told you he has "no idea of the market size" for his new toothbrush and "no idea how many we'll sell." Is that a strategy that marketing leaders should emulate-or just the privilege of a sole owner speaking to you from his superyacht?

Katie: Although Dyson owns 100% of this company, he stepped away from the CEO role some time ago. I imagine other people at the firm do have some knowledge of market size and sales projections; clearly, they need to know enough to plan media, retail placement, and the like.

Still, Dyson has failed before-most recently with its electric car, which was scrapped after years and years in development when the market shifted and it became commercially unviable to put into production.

Marketers, and really anybody in business, could learn to have a Dyson approach to quitting, developing a sense of knowing when to pull the plug and, crucially, standing by the decision. But I'm aware it's probably much easier to do that when you work for a private company.

You report that the $499 toothbrush requires a special Dyson toothpaste. Would it be cynical to suspect that there is a business model here, similar to the classic example of a razor brand that makes all its money on blade refills?

Katie: Perhaps! This isn't actually Dyson's first move into consumer packaged goods: It makes hair-care products designed to be used with its hair dryers and hair wraps. But the non-foaming aspect of the toothpaste is more critical to this product because regular toothpaste can obscure the view of the CameraJet's camera, according to the company.

I personally think Dyson will concentrate on finding interesting ways to sell the CameraJet to different audiences (will it break through into FSA eligibility, perhaps? Could it partner with a gut-health company and go after the longevity crowd?) rather than bank on making money from toothpaste, a strategy that doesn't feel very true to a brand that's all about innovation.
Define 'Zero'
Nonzero alcohol content in some nonalcoholic beers is fueling a push for clarity in the fast-growing sector, the WSJ Leadership Institute's Jennifer Williams writes.

Regulators draw a strict line: "Nonalcoholic" drinks can include up to 0.5% alcohol by volume, while "alcohol-free" beverages must contain no trace. Some brands use terms such as "0% alcohol" interchangeably with "nonalcoholic," however, leaving the details to the fine print.

That's a nonissue for most people, according to Bill Shufelt, CEO and co-founder of Athletic Brewing, the largest dedicated nonalcoholic brewer. "Consumers are not looking for it, and if they are, they don't care enough about it to switch off of their brands," Shufelt said.
But the share of consumers who do care isn't exactly 0.0%, either.
Expectant mothers and the organ-transplant community are increasingly debating the risks of nonalcoholic drinks.
To protect brand trust, the Adult Non-Alcoholic Beverage Association advises members to leave off claims like "zero" and "alcohol-free" from any drink with trace booze.

"When you're assuming there are zero traces of alcohol in it and then you find out that there are some, even though they're very minute, it catches some consumers by surprise," said Marcos Salazar, CEO of the association.
Some brands are already adapting. CleanCo reformulated its alcohol-free cocktails and spirits to hit an absolute 0.0% ABV after its market testing revealed shoppers were confused by trace amounts.

The Magic Number

Price of the smart glasses being introduced by Snap this month, nearly a decade after its Spectacles started piling up unsold in warehouses. CEO Evan Spiegel since then has advised the marketing team to rebrand the unit as Specs and urged a more sophisticated presentation, eschewing the company's signature yellow.
